utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Do you hear me well, Mr. Galic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you perfectly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin today there seems to be a housekeeping matter from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you, Your Honours. Just a correction for the exhibit list. 65 ter number 1D01473 which was admitted as Exhibit D3402 should in fact be Exhibit D3410. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you okay, Mr. Tieger, to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General Galic.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I again have to remind both you and I to make pauses, to speak slowly, and in addition I would kindly ask you to give me as short answers as possible because I'm going to focus only on the essence so as we can finish as soon as possible. General, we were discussing the topic of fire coming from the city and your responses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 1D01530. That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please explain one thing to us. The date is the 15th of May, 1993, and in paragraph 1, fourth passage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It looks like the English version is not, in fact, the English version. What we have in English is the translation of a different document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the date is the 12th of May. While we are waiting for the English translation, may I continue with my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have an English translation at all, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, so it seems that we do not have the English translation at the moment. Shall we collapse the English and let's see how we can deal with this. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, concerning the 15th of May, you are reporting to the Main Staff that there was fire open on your positions from Dobrinja 1 and 3, that's in paragraph 3, and then again from Mojmilo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Given that we do not have English translation, why don't you ask the witness to read out the relevant passage.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we might be able to help. Mr. Reid has just been able to locate a translation which he can print up now and we can put on the ELMO, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please focus on the fourth paragraph which says: "From the area of Bistrik our positions at Bistrik Kula and Vidikovac were targeted and ten 82-millimetre shells fell. Also hit were the areas of Mrkovici." You said that you did not fire back except in the area of Ilijas where you managed to repel the attack. As for Bistrik Kula, you say that you neutralised enemy positions in Bistrik with four shells. Why was that, given that you were targeted by ten shells?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the report relating to this specific date - now I see the second page in the Serbian - but I know what this is about and I understand your question, therefore I can give you an answer regardless of what page we are looking at. The point was that they were opening fire from the area of Bistrik from mortars aiming at our Bistrik Kula and Vidikovac, and that is correct. These are the positions that we held. Nevertheless, we responded with half the strength - let's put it that way - compared to the number of shells that they fired. In response to their eight shells we fired four. The main reason was because Bistrik was densely populated and any attempt to neutralise would raise the issue of proportionality and the use of weapons in such a populated area. Now, where the exact location of targets in Bistrik were, whether it was in a park or further away from civilians, we can consider that in general terms. But in short, I would say that that was a selective way of responding and a positive proportionate one carried out with a view to their fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Item 7 says that there were two wounded and a woman was wounded in Grbavica from a sniper. Was this something usual or was it something special?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at a number of reports, one can say that this was one of the more quiet days in that period. In the area covered by the Ilijas Brigade there were intensive operations and they were actively involved in them rather than in opening fire.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3411.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now 1D01534.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Good morning. Could we please have a copy of the English translation which has the date of the 15th of May. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No doubt that will be uploaded on e-court very soon. Could you confirm that, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Reid has already e-mailed it to Defence so that they can upload it. And in the interim we have the hard copy that was on the ELMO, and Mr. Piletta-Zanin can certainly have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can keep it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we have skipped four days. Now we are on the 19th of May, and under number 1 you said that they violated the truce once again. Was that the period of truce when you were exposed to this fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this report shows exactly the locations and times and the weapons used to violate the truce started from Hadzici, Ilijas, Rajlovac, and all other areas covered by the 1st Romanija Brigade. So this was the time of cease-fire, and I ordered that exact reports be sent to the Main Staff regarding the breaches of the cease-fire so that they can have information when they go to meet with UNPROFOR or with the mixed commission that met almost on a regular basis. And you know very well that representatives of the VRS attended the meetings of this mixed committee, mainly those from the Main Staff, also representatives of the BH Army and their Main Staff, and UNPROFOR commanders for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up the English version so that we can see this portion relating to Ilidza where it says that artillery fire came from Mojmilo and rifle grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And twice you say here that you did not respond. There was even sniping fire but you still did not respond. Can you tell me why didn't you respond?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's clear from this report why we did not respond because they had an order not to fire back whenever there was any provocation. It is difficult to say at this moment how justified it was for a person not to respond if his life is threatened. Nevertheless, there was such an order and all the soldiers and officers abided by this order strictly, although there was some individuals who didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the Serbian version --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, we need the next page, page 2 in the Serbian. Let's see what happens with the English version. Maybe we need to change it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, item under 2 you can see what the corps did, that it improved the defence lines, carried out observations, enhanced fortifications --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters were not able to hear you in full. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under item 2 you can see the report about what the corps was doing, a number of corps officers went to tour the units in order to monitor how the cease-fire was being observed. Can you explain what this means?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we issued an order to cease hostilities and fire, the corps command members went on the ground to check the situation and verify whether they were observing and abiding by the order. The corps command was not a large one, it was not manned to the full, but always a number of officers, including myself, we always went to the ground in order to see how the units were behaving and whether they were abiding by the orders. This is particularly important because if there was such an extensive enemy activity, both in terms of their actions and fire, it was necessary for us to assess how to proceed because on the spot we were unable to reach a proper and appropriate decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under 7 you see that you lost two soldiers, two children were seriously wounded, and five were lightly wounded [as interpreted]. And sub-item (b) says that your prediction is that the violations of cease-fire will continue in order to provoke conflicts and with the aim of blaming the VRS. Can you tell the Chamber how did these military and civilian casualties affect the status of cease-fire and the psychological state of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, any loss of life or any casualties, especially during cease-fire, causes even great anxiety and some undesirable reactions. We can see that in this particular instance there were children who were casualties and this is very upsetting for the soldiers because these are the children of those soldiers who were waging war. Those were their children, and it is only natural that it had an impact, both on the soldiers and the civilians and the general atmosphere. Under such circumstances it is very difficult to maintain cease-fire and to achieve peace. We wanted to achieve peace. It was ordered for us to achieve peace, but you see that we found ourselves in a situation where it was very difficult to decide what to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3412, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have 1D01539. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of May you are reporting in a regular combat report at 1700 hours to the Main Staff that in Hadzici sector a tank fired five shells on the centre of Hadzici and Ilidza and Nedzarici from rifle grenades and in Vogosca from the direction of Pretis and the transportation faculty there was intensive sniper fire. A bit further down it says in the Grbavica sector throughout the day civilian targets were fired on, in particular the green market more than 30, 82-millimetre shells and on the Slavisa Vajner Cica Barracks they fired by rifle grenades and sniper fire. Intensive fire on Sucura houses. Can you tell us, General, whether there were any military assets at the market that would justify the firing at the market?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at this report in its entirety we can see that in the area there were activities targeting Trebevic as well. Let us not forget that. Under item 2, that was why these activities from the area from Miljacka also including fire, so from there to the market in Grbavica were an integral part of the overall operations. I think that after this incident I went to the green market. There were no military targets or military forces at the market or any military assets that were situated right there on the market. It's not a big market but rather a small one, and in practice it could not operate. Whenever I visited there were few people and they didn't have much produce to sell. So that the green market could not have been in operation. I'm not sure if there could have been one or two stalls that were open after that. Whether there was any reason to target it, in my personal view and from what I personally learned there was no reason whatsoever to target the small green market in Grbavica at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the following page so that we can see item 7 and see you had three slightly wounded soldiers, one seriously wounded, one soldier was killed and one civilian was killed. Under item 8 it says that you observed the cease-fire and that you opened fire only in defence when responding to the enemy fire. How did you manage to maintain discipline so that the responses would only be made to respond to the fire that you received?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in all the war situations when there are such active operations and fire, as there was on this particular day, including the area up towards, as I already said, our central zone, the parts of Grbavica that we held you also visited the area down there. You know what the situation was like. You have to descend between Debelo Brdo and Hrasno Brdo in order to reach it, so it's as if you're entering hell; that's how it looked. Up there, there were some tents that were blocking the area so that it couldn't be targeted by snipers, and holding your position in that Grbavica was really difficult and it was difficult to withstand because we were encircled in a way. How did we manage to maintain some sort of truce? Well, we only responded to active fire. Where the forces managed to penetrate and were supported along the axis of their penetration, we had to respond because by that date they threatened the lives in the zone and probably all our positions would later be threatened as well of some brigade units or parts of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. There were instances when they cut off the road leading from Lukavica towards Pale on Trebevic mountain, and that was practically the only road leading towards Pale and in-depth towards Republika Srpska. If it were cut off, then Lukavica was encircled. Up until around the 14th of August, 1993, after that the situation was somewhat better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see page 2 in English and page 1 of -- 1 in B/C/S. Item number 2. The first part of item number 2 reads as: "Our forces are at the lines reached. An enemy attack in Trebevic area was successfully repulsed, destroying one of" the guns and et cetera. But the third part of the item 2 says: "No firing by our forces ..." So how do we read this report? Can I take it that any fires in defensive action would not be recorded as any firing in your report? Could you clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Your Honour. Here is how this is to be understood. We are covering the entire zone. The areas where there was no need to respond fire, then we didn't. Where there were active operations and where they penetrated our lines we had to respond. That was the situation which is later on explained in the rest of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it at that. We'll admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3413, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, on the 1st of June something happened for which I am charged and I believe so are you; namely, the incident was when two shells were fired on a group of around 200 people who were watching a football game on a parking-lot, which was surrounded on three sides by residential buildings and the fourth side was a road leading to Lukavica, and so on and so forth. That was on the 1st of June, 1993. In your statement in the chapter entitled "Indictment incidents," you say: [In English] "I never received an order to open fire at these locations on these dates. Also, I never issued an order that fire be opened at these locations on these dates and I never informed the superior command that fire was opened at these locations on these dates." [Interpretation] General, do you remember and did you learn later during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. What statement did you refer to, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Proofing notes, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This proofing note was not admitted as kind of Rule 92 ter. You should put your question directly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you remember this incident and do you remember whether on that day you received an order from superior commands or issue an order to subordinated commands to open fire at a football match?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though the question was 50 per cent in English and 50 per cent in Serbian, that was the interpretation I received, I know what this is about and I know what I'm supposed to answer. Because mainly in the corps zone whatever happened I was familiar with it more or less. It was the 1st of June, 1993. We have seen earlier that in this period there was a sort of cease-fire or truce or cessation of hostilities. I cannot say precisely what that was, but more or less that is what it was. Now, whether in this period fire was opened from the area of Dobrinja that was something we reported on earlier about this fire coming from Dobrinja at our positions. Nearby, close to the place where the incident took place, as far as I can remember - as it was 20 years ago after all - there was an atomic shelter and the atomic shelter was supposed to be used by civilians; however, it was used to shelter soldiers and materiel from the recoilless guns which were withdrawn towards Mojmilo including the PAMs and other pieces of equipment and troops. So it was one of the military targets which it was justified and legitimate target at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to stop for a moment. I thought not to call up this document, but perhaps if it will refresh your memory. D340 is the document that we need. It's a Defence document, D340, your report dated the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's no problem for me to tell you about the incident, so I accept the situation in which I would answer such questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, please continue.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to realise that the incident happened at the confrontation line, perhaps 150 metres in-depth from the confrontation line at the positions of the BH Army. So it's not so deep really. If we remember the map, the colour map which we called up, when we see the deployment of forces of, including the Army of BH and the 5th Brigade in the Dobrinja area, then we will see that in that area forces of the strength of one battalion were deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now focus on the first page where it says where the enemy fired from in the sector of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade with mortars 220- and 80-millimetres [as interpreted], no extraordinary events. Can we please see the following page both in the Serbian and the English so that we can see the conclusion. In the conclusion you say that the forces of the corps fully observed the order with regard to the cease-fire. We have not responded to enemy provocations, and we expect further intense fire of enemy snipers at civilian targets. If you had fired a single shell or the two that I talked about, would they be included in this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, can we just go back to what Dr. Karadzic has read in from this document, and it's at lines 3 and 4 on page 14. Dr. Karadzic referred to the document as referring to 220-millimetre mortars and 80-millimetre mortars, and the document reads: "The enemy fired 120-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortars on the area of Zlatiste to Osmice and Krtelji in the area of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a matter of interpretation and the transcript. Thank you for the intervention. I read it out correctly, but let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, General, about this conclusion that you did not respond to provocations. If you had fired a single shell or two shells or more, would that be included in your report as an obligation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we said resolutely where and why we responded, I don't see any reason, as in this particular situation we did not know what was going on there. I didn't know. I learned about this when I came here to the Tribunal. So if we had fired or had been active in that area, I suppose that it would have to be included in this report. There is no reason why it wouldn't be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This has been admitted earlier. Can we now please call up 1D10512. General, you have said that you prohibited civilian gatherings even further away from the line. How do you see this organisation of a football match with 200 viewers at the confrontation line itself?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our zone, the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in particular --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've been trying to find a translation of this document. Do we not have one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that we still have not received the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then you should properly put foundation about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies, that's precisely what I'm doing. We have seen in documents and General told us that he prohibited civilians gathering in the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Now I'm asking the General how as a soldier he views this fact that football match was organised at the confrontation line by the other side. Was that allowed and how responsible was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's not a proper foundational question, with respect, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What this document is about, who wrote it, we should know that in order to understand the document and the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not reached the document yet, Your Excellencies. I asked the General what his attitude was and his orders about civilians gathering or rallying and in -- especially in view of the order on the cease-fire, and then I will move on to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic, with respect, can take the document away so that the witness is not led to his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can remove it until the witness answers. Can we then remove it, please. I haven't read out anything from the document, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you answer, General, what was your attitude to the gathering of civilians, grouping of civilians, and their activities in the zone that was within reach of the enemy artillery?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very gladly, Mr. President. I will gladly answer. I just waited to see when I could do so, when I would be allowed to do so. In our zone, due to the losses which we have seen earlier and due to the general conditions that we had in the zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, we took a series of measures in order to protect our civilians or civilians in general, civilians who were in our zone. One of the measures for sure was to prohibit a great number of people gathering together. As for transportation by public city transportation, we allocated specific positions that should be sheltered where people could wait because we could see that bus stops were targeted. And then people would be transported from such designated locations further on, whether they were going from Ilidza or from Hadzici or from the area of Lukavica or Vojkovici and Grbavica. Another thing that we did was remove the civilians who were living right next to the confrontation line, remove them somewhere in-depth as much as possible, because we did not have as many civilian buildings and facilities in our zone as the BH Army did. But we had quite enough because we should know that in the area of the 1st Corps of the BH Army there were 350.000 civilians living, and on our side perhaps 100- or 120.000. So it was necessary to move them all and to ensure a degree of protection for them. The buildings housing civilians, we told them to somehow cover the windows facing the front line, that's a normal thing, because I know what we did only at my command, where the seat of the command was, or rather, the forward command post in Lukavica. We had to place the big metal sheets and other shelters to protect officers, even though officers were still targeted in the premises where we worked. We expected that the same thing would be done by the 1st Corps of the BH Army. Therefore, I would never have expected that someone would involve in a football match and say that it was very difficult, that there was sniper fire and it was impossible to live, and then we would go out and play football 150 metres from the confrontation line. For me, this is something not normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On that day did you get an order from the superior command to shoot? What -- did you forward it to the lower levels and did you inform the Main Staff of the events?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see from the previous report, neither did I get an order to open fire in the area, nor did I order any such thing or receive a report that fire had been opened on that day. In a word, I couldn't send a report about shooting in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: D34 -- no, could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D10512, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us the places -- the place names I'm going to read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic should take the document away if he's not going to address the document. This is giving the witness a chance to prepare himself for the answer that's -- he's going to be asked to give.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the document is very clear. I want to ask the document [as interpreted] where certain places are that the SRK targeted, whether they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We do not -- we cannot read this document while you can. So please introduce the document first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I want to do, but let's have it on the screen. This is a report -- or perhaps the witness can introduce the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it on my screen, sorry. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be coming, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document, tell us what it is, tell us its date, and what does the document say?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before. Let me take a look at it. It's a document of the Igman operational group. They belonged to the 1st Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dated?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I see Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to be extremely accurate. There's something missing, both in the English translation and the French translation. I don't wish to waste any time. I heard the General saying in his language that it was the first time in his life that he saw this document; in other words he saw this document for the first time today. If I have made a mistake, General Galic will say so, but that is, at any rate, what I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I heard that as well. That will be reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's actually already reflected on line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say it's dated the 1st of June, and item 1 says what the Serbs targeted. Tell us about these places: Drniste, Crni Vrh, Grebak, Rogoj. Where are these places in relation to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you ask the witness to read out the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aloud?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read the first paragraph out aloud.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be glad to: "The Chetniks," obviously they are referring to the Army of Republika Srpska, "during this day shelled the line in the area of responsibility of the 4th," this should read brigade, "the 4th Motorised Brigade," I can't see it all too well, "the 81st Mountain Brigade (along the line Drniste-Crni Vrh-Grebak and Rogoj. The Chetniks are fortified ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to continue. Please tell us where these places are.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rogoj is towards Kalinovik. It's not in the Sarajevo area at all. From Trnovo to Kalinovik there is a pass by the name of Rogoj. Grebak is somewhere between Sarajevo and Gorazde. It's also like a pass -- actually, it's a plateau. It was very important for them at the time because there was a reloading station there. I can continue to explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just tell us how far Grebak is from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe some 20-odd kilometres. I never really measured. That's the distance from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the last sentence of item II, please read it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just finish the first paragraph before we move on, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We can't read it, Mr. Karadzic, otherwise we can't understand it. So could you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no interest to read this out because it's irrelevant. Once the translation is in, you can read it. I just want to show what the SRK targeted because the General said that they didn't target the city. These targets were 20 kilometres from the town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just in case, how do we know that you omitted something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the translation arrives you will see. It's irrelevant. We're just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm, Mr. President, that nothing important has been skipped here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But having heard Ms. Edgerton's request, there's -- I see no difficulty reading out the first paragraph. Could you read out the remainder of the first paragraph, starting from the 81st - where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you continue with the part after Grebak and Rogoj.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem: "The Chetniks are fortifying the line," does this say Galica," Galica-Kosuta and the line Katelj-Korijen. In the Hadzici-Zunovnica area, during the night Chetnik activities were enhanced especially in the form of movement of vehicles between the Zunovnica Barracks and Drozgometva," I think, "no significant movements in the area of the 81st Mountain Brigade." That was item I. I can move on to item II. If need be, I can read that out too. I can also tell you where these positions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not necessary. In paragraph II they are discussing their own forces?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this part where they are speaking about the Chetniks referring to our forces. Gosuta and Katelj are further in the direction of Gorazde, so even further than Grebak. Korijen, or rather, Hadzici -- Zunovnica is a warehouse in the Hadzici area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just read out the last sentence of paragraph II, if you will, General.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A part of the unused units celebrated a Bajram holiday by engaging in sports competitions and other activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we set up a connection between this information and the event at Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're going to go further into this document, I'd like to have it read out because based on my pathetic understanding of the language it looks like this passage that Dr. Karadzic has just had the witness read out is connected to forces in the region of -- moving in the direction of Gorazde. So to avoid any misapprehension or misinterpretation about untranslated documents perhaps we could profit from the witness being here and have him read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all respect, Bajram is on the same day, both on Igman and on Dobrinja. And the forces going to Igman have to pass through Dobrinja, through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, first of all, we have to establish this, for example. I will ask the witness on your behalf, Mr. Karadzic. Could we know from this document when it was written and when it was sent and received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see when it was sent out. It was sent out on the 1st of June, 1993. The time of reception, I don't see it well. I can only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you see the top line, it says Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the right-hand side it reads, time of reception 07, then it's not very clear. I may not have the right glasses. 24 -- I suppose -- yes. Oh, on the 07th at 24 hours and 10 minutes. I suppose that that's what they wrote. It says, 07.24.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read the first line as well which says Sarajevo something, 2nd of June. Does it signify the day of receipt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes. Sarajevo, the 2nd of June, 1993, number 6680, then file name. This was probably taken out of an electronic file DADE260A and so on. So this is a report of the 2nd of June. It was sent out on the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me just add it was sent by the Igman operative group to the command of the 1st Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the area of responsibility of that Igman operation group cover the football field we were discussing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The zone of responsibility of the Igman operative group does not cover it. In the operational sense it may but in the combat sense it doesn't cover Dobrinja because Igman covers Mount Igman and the area towards Rogoj and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did the units of the 1st Corps leave Sarajevo and where did they go? I mean the Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a known fact. Once the VRS in June 1992 surrendered the airport, then that airport --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But please be brief. Did it happen that units left the city core?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left Dobrinja and that part of Sarajevo and went to Igman, especially in the Butmir area and on toward Hrasnica, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the reverse direction?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, from Igman to Butmir and through the airport toward Dobrinja. That was a direction that -- along which they moved for a while without a tunnel. And later around the 15th of August, 1993, the tunnel was completed and we know that they were digging that tunnel throughout 1993, although the UNPROFOR and others were trying to convince us that nothing was being dug.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You must understand that I must try and save some time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, or rather, marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3414, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see 1D01551. 1D01551. Oh, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a regular combat report drafted at 1700 hours. Four 120-millimetre projectiles were fired at Vojkovici. Were all the reports as detailed as this one? Why didn't they say five projectiles? Why is it four?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the reports that we have seen so far show that these reports were rather precise with regard to the quantity and type of ammunitions fired, both from our side and on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us very briefly what is Vojkovici.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a suburb at the foot of Mount Igman in the direction of Hrasnica. The Zeljeznica river separates it from the rest of town, so it's at the foot of Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see that a tank fired at Vogosca. Now tell us what the connection is between reconnoitring and observation with adequate response to enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't see any reference in what we have on the screen to a tank firing at Vogosca. I don't think that's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We see 82-millimetre shells. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "At Vraca and Grbavica with a tank and a recoilless gun."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But not at Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Vogosca was 82-millimetres, 25, 82-millimetre shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we have the next page in English before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- is there any connection between reconnaissance and observation and an appropriate response?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without good reconnaissance and observation with regard to the origin of fire and what kind of fire was used and what the assessment and the targets were, then a decision is made about what response would be appropriate. Throughout the week I have been telling you what an appropriate or adequate response would be, and we tried as much as possible to counter it with the identical weapon. If they used infantry fire, we would respond with infantry fire. If they used recoilless gun, since we didn't have any we had to use some other weapons such as mortars, et cetera, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page I think in the both version -- versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under item 7 you say that you have two fatalities among your soldiers and another seven were wounded and in conclusion you say that the prediction is that they will not observe the cease-fire. So that means that in this period cease-fire was in force as well?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see but it was nearing the end because there were many violations and we assumed, judging by these activities, that the BH Army was going to continue to breach the cease-fire and that they were already infiltrating sabotage and terrorist groups in the area of the corps and they did that quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3415, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just with the note that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- the witness -- Dr. Karadzic has addressed the questions about this document to the witness as though the document was his own, and just for the record the document does not have his signature on it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we heard from the witness, although in respect of other documents, how the documents were signed by his Chief of Staff on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so, just to note that this is a document that is not the witness's document. It's a document signed by his Chief of Staff so that the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was referring to the corps command not to the General in person. Can we now please have 1D01555. This is dated 24th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by your command and we can see your name at the end. Let us look at paragraph 1 where it says that they fired from a distance from artillery weapons at civilian residential areas and you name them, and then you say that fire was returned and an enemy gun was hit from a multiple rocket-launcher. Did you retaliate by firing on their targets?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this report dated the 24th of June, 1993, you can see which targets they selected to fire on. But we responded only by firing at the area of Hrasnica which is where the depot was. This is just below Mount Igman and I don't know if there are any residential areas at all [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, which positions did you select and which targets did you select to fire on?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we were in a position to make a selection and neutralise military targets, we always opened fire at places where there were no residential areas and where the origins of fire were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3416, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to skip a few weeks again. Can we now please have 1D01561.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this report sent at 1700 hours on the 5th of July, 1993. How do you estimate and assess this activity? We can see where -- infantry fire, rifle grenades, howitzers, 105 mortars and their targets. So the whole item 1, can you please take a look at it and explain what kind of activities is being described here and what is UNPROFOR doing across the airport?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look only at some of the activities, I don't think it's necessary to read all of it, you can see that the whole area of the Sarajevo front there was intense activity on the part of the enemy targeting Faletici, Mrkovici, Nedzarici, Dobrinja, Kasindolska Street, and of course there were always snipers firing at Grbavica or other areas and in this instance they were firing from Stupska junction. So if you want me, I can read everything. For example, there were five 82-mortar shells fired at Vogosca, and so on and so forth. So the whole front line in the Sarajevo battle-field was covered by this situation and by their activities. It was interesting to note what it says about what UNPROFOR was doing and I'm going to read it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later because that's a separate topic. In the transcript in lines 10 and 11 the witness said that the whole battle-field was on fire. What did you mean by saying that it was on fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was under infantry, artillery, all other kind of fires, and this is a military term to say that it was on fire. It's a customary word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what your units were doing which is described under item 2?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our units, I think, were preparing themselves in this period, that is to say on the Sarajevo front line and in the direction of Sarajevo. Our wish was to calm the situation to a certain extent and to keep it to -- under control. Our units were not active and were not targeting Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the next page, item 7, losses. We also need the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please just tell me what is your opinion about the losses incurred on that day. Item 7 you have fatalities and wounded. You don't need to read it. Just tell us what kind of losses you suffered.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that several soldiers were both killed and wounded. I don't see here that there were any casualties among civilians, but when you have this kind of fire and this kind of activities, it is inevitable that civilians also suffer casualties. But why it didn't happen in this instance? That is interesting. I'm going to explain to you. When we were compiling this report and it was done by another chief of mine, Colonel Milosevic, he must have waited for another day in order to get information and report from the civilian authorities relating to the number of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3417, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In my indictment, General, there is an incident which allegedly took place on the 12th of July, 1993. But before that, can you tell us at the time when you drafted this previous document was cease-fire in force?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that cease-fire was still in force, but I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether on the 11th, 12th, or 13th of July, 1993, you issued an order to open mortar fire on residential buildings on the streets of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the names of the streets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the street name, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hakija Turajlic Street, formerly the alley of Branko Bulic, and in the residential area of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in those days did you issue an order to this effect or did you receive any order that your forces opened mortar fire at these targets?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to establish a correlation between this and the situation that prevailed in the corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid it will take too much time. Can you tell us briefly: Did you open fire in this specific period, targeting these residential areas?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this being done with regard to residential areas because at that time I was elsewhere engaged on a different assignment and we're going to speak about this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your subordinate commands inform you about opening fire without any order of yours? Did they open fire at all?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they did not report any such activities. I still see the previous report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report which is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we now have P2665.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we wait we can look for another document.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think this is 11th of August. I made a mistake about the date. Now under item 1, what is being ordered? Please read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1, I find it a bit hard to read but I'll do my best: "I order do not open fire against the city of Sarajevo ..." But there's something missing here, "at any cost." It must read: Do not open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, if you look at the words "Sarajevo," look how many letters there are.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you are right, Mr. President, your sight is better than mine. It reads: "Do not open fire," whereas here the word "not" is glued to the word "Sarajevo" and I know that no one could have issued any different order. So it reads: "Do not open fire against the city of Sarajevo at any cost."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpreters and the translators understood it properly. How often did you issue this kind of orders and what were your instructions and orders from the Main Staff and the Presidency with regard to opening fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning opening fire on the city, I know that at the time when I assumed my duties there were already certain orders in place issued by the civilian authorities. I don't know if they were issued by you yourself, but I know that they had come from the civilian authorities and I know that the Supreme Command also issued said authorities. And on various occasions we received such orders from higher commands and we discussed these orders on the very first day when Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali came. So there was no need to issue this kind of orders every single day because they were orders that were applicable for a longer period of time and were only renewed if the situation changed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D1564, please. 1D1564, please. Yes, this is what I wanted to call up the first time too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is there no translation of this document again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sent for translation quite a long time ago. Whether we received a translation yet or not I'm not quite sure -- no, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Reid has done his magic again and we have a hard copy that can go on the ELMO. So this was previously translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please tell us what your units were doing on the 11th of July. You do not need to read it, but just tell us what they were doing, what were their activities and along which axes?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, in the area of this front in Sarajevo, if I can put it that way, the enemy mainly stayed on the lines reached and we prevented him from penetrating in particular towards Igman. There were manoeuvres of forces towards Igman and the surrounding area in the remaining part of the front at the time Lukavac 93 operation was underway. It had begun between the 6th and the 7th of June, 1993, and that was why we had other operations along the axis Jahorina-Trnovo-Hojta-Igman-Bjelasnica, and another axis, that is to say on this one where the Main Corps forces in co-ordinated action with the Herzegovina Corps and the Drina Corps, and the other corps axis was along Hadzici-Igman, that is to say Hadzici-Tresnjevo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any active operations towards the inner ring?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read all of this but judging by the situation it was no -- it was not necessary to engage in any active operations towards the centre of the city, the inner city, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now please have 65 ter 23885 so that we can see what your forces were doing on the day of the incident itself, that is the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the Serbian version as well so that the witness can read it. We do not need the one dated the 11th of July, but the Serbian version of the document of the 12th of July, that's 23885 under 65 ter. The English version is the right one and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be coming.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. If we can just zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were the preoccupations of the corps command and where did it carry out operations on that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could the witness just be asked the question and not shown the document? If the question was: What were the preoccupations of the corps command, the witness is clearly taking an expansive read of the document as displayed in front of him before he answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hold on a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just strictly speaking the Chamber agrees with Ms. Edgerton, but once we are dealing with war situation in general the Chamber has no difficulty with putting the report or orders issued by the witness to the witness. But however, when we have new areas, I would like you to put some foundational questions before you put the documents to the witness. I think it's -- unless it is inconvenient, we shall take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can just finish this document in a minute and I accept the suggestions and decisions. But it seems to me that with the previous document General Galic said what follows from this document, mainly along which axes his corps was engaged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. My answer defined precisely what I was now asked, even before the document was called up. I apologise for saying so, but that's true. And I would not have answered differently in any way whatsoever than as I already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us whether in this part "I order," in the end did you order any fire or any activities directed against the city?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that time - and that was the 12th of July - I think that there wasn't so much directed against the city but against Hrasnica, yes, that zone there. I cannot really see this well, I cannot read it, so I cannot use this document. But as far as my memory serves me well, I think that we had reached Trnovo and we were supposed to go there with the majority of the forces. I'm not sure if we were there already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please try and read it and see whether you ordered activities directed against Dobrinja. You see it in the last passage.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it but I don't have to read it. I don't think that I ordered anything like that because there was no reason for that. No, that's not it. If we can please scroll down a little bit, I need the text. Yes. Urgently and at the latest by -- continue the operation. Lukavac 93 is being continued as I ordered. Free the Trnovo-Kijevo-Sarajevo road. That's up in the direction of Trnovo and it was part of the Lukavac 93 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no mention of Dobrinja here as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3419, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I have finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the break, if you allow me, I would like to say as far as the rest of the proceedings is concerned I'm not quite sure of what the translation says regarding Mr. Galic's testimony. Line 24 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Piletta-Zanin repeat the line and the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you kindly repeat the page and line numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, sir. Page 29, line 4 and following, lines 4 to 8 or 9.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see. The General did not say, "I do not know whether there was," but he said, "I don't know that there was any civilian place of residence there." [In English] "I didn't know that there were any," not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can listen to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, I'll read out what you are recorded as having said. This is a question and answer about the firing at the area of Hrasnica. So I will -- quote, this is your answer: "If you look at this report dated the 24th of June, 1993, you can see which targets they selected to fire on. But responded only by firing at the area of Hrasnica which is where the depot was. This is just below Mount Igman and I don't know if there are any residential areas at all." Do you remember having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's mostly that. It was so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to add something. It was fired on the facilities of the depot up there, which is practically outside of Hrasnica and below Igman. This is why I said -- I'm not sure whether I have made myself sufficiently clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put you again. Do you know whether there's any residential area or not below Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are some residential areas below Igman. There is the Hrasnica residential area and other areas towards the airport, but where the depot was fired on then, towards Igman, there aren't any. I don't remember that there are any houses or buildings there apart from the depot itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 35 minutes and resume at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we get back to business and move on, I just wanted to raise one matter with respect to the documents that we dealt with today which -- where the OTP, Mr. Reid, in fact, was able to find English translations and that's D3411 and D3418. Now, in respect of D3418, Dr. Karadzic clearly said it was sent for translation quite a long time ago and appeared to be blaming CLSS for there not being a translation available. Now, Your Honours, my understanding of how the document management and translation system works is that these requests go through the ODM, the Office of Document Management, where they're screened for content and by ERN number to see whether or not a translation exists. And generally within a few hours, ODM is able to notify the requesting party as to whether a document has been translated or not. Now, after Dr. Karadzic made that remark we were able to see that both translations for these documents were actually completed in the summer of 2001. So it seems to me, Your Honour, if - as Dr. Karadzic said - these had been requested quite a long time ago they would have received quite a long time ago the existing translations of these documents. So in light of that I would actually like to encourage Dr. Karadzic to be a little bit more careful in choosing his words when he appears to cast blame on somebody when it comes to these untranslated documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have anything in response, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just so much, Your Excellencies, that I did not have that specific document in mind but that we send regularly everything that we want to call up to be translated. I didn't mean this particular document, but the documents that we need in general we send them to be translated. We do not wait for the last moment to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I would like you to be precise in making a specific statement in relation to a specific statement. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, now that we dwelt on this incident and in general incidents about which protests were lodged with you or that you were informed about by the UNPROFOR, what did you do with regard to this? Did you respond to them and on the basis of what did you respond if you did?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of whether the UNPROFOR lodged a protest with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, it depended on what that was about, what incident it was. They protested some incidents; they didn't protest others. As for sniping incidents, I do not remember a single protest that was lodged just because of a sniping incident. As for the shelling or mortar fire, as there is no artillery fire in enclosure 2 of the indictment, then I think that sometimes, perhaps once or twice, we did receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if you learned from the media or from their protest, did you then check that on the basis of what did you state whether that was fire coming from your unit or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we learned that an incident did occur in various ways, whether through the media or whether because of a protest note or because we were informed through the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, we at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had a man who was assigned for co-operation with UNPROFOR, that was Mr. Indjic who was representative of the Main Staff and at the same time the representative of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and he was in charge of co-operation with UNPROFOR in the Sarajevo area and even further afield. If we received such information, we then checked it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D43084 is the next document that we would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And as for your answer, I wanted to say that the shortest answers are also the best, General. 1D43084. And we would need the English version as well, please. General, can you please focus on this document and tell me whether you're familiar with it and tell us what was the purpose of this document.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was delivered to all units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and it's basically an order to submit a report on the following: Who opened fire from artillery and mortars at the town of Sarajevo or from any weapon with a calibre exceeding 12.7 millimetres. The report must contain the following information: Who ordered the fire and who approved it. That is similar to what we have already discussed, but this is now more precise. You remember when I spoke about the use of artillery, this is similar, but this includes all other weapons too. So who ordered the fire and who approved it. At what time fire was opened and in which sector? And here, as usual, I point out that they're duty-bound to act upon this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a minute ago that you checked. What has this document to do with the checking of the alleged activity?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is dated the 11th of June. All our orders to subordinate units had to be checked in a certain manner to know whether they were being acted upon, to what extent, and so on. This is a strong order imposing obligations on all units, obligations connected with activity directed against the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we know who signed the document on the General's behalf? It's not the General's document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you know -- do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember the signatures of authorised persons, I think that was the operations officer's signature, Mr. Cedo Sladoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But based on all other elements, can you tell that this is a document of your command?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we consider all elements, it was processed and delivered by the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I'm not sure who actually signed it, but once such an order is received it must urgently be forwarded to the units. When I'm not there then somebody else present from the command will sign. But such an order must be transmitted urgently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a question for both parties. When we have an English translation of a B/C/S document, you would usually have the handwritten part translated as well, but this time I'm not sure which is translation of which. If anybody could assist us in this regard.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down the original. The upper right-hand part is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But maybe you can help us, General, so we can read the section under the stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Delivered to the Vogosca Brigade at 9.50, they made a remark of the fact that it was delivered to the Vogosca Brigade at 9.50.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it reads: Delivered to all units?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise the signature under this handwritten remark about the Vogosca Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could it be someone from the Vogosca Brigade as proof of reception?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possibly. But this is actually the processing of the cable so it may have been someone who worked on that, but I don't remember the man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just for everyone's information, I'm told that the translation was provided by General Galic's Defence counsel in his first trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given -- and the font I assumed so that English version came from another trial and the Defence was able to locate the original. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll continue with July. Can we please see 1D1567.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on this report which I'll summarise for us to go faster. From Igman there was firing at the Vojkovici neighbourhood and the Famos factory where 15, 82-millimetre and 120-millimetre mortar shells were -- fell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Dr. Karadzic doesn't need to summarise the document. We can see it here in both languages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what this day was like considering losses too and what do you do under paragraph 2? Your units opened fire at selected targets. What follows from this document?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, if we look at this document, we see that enemy forces often opened fire on our units in Sarajevo. Here it is also precisely said from which sectors and at which features they fire. This is around the 18th of July - I believe a report will also show that - that the main forces of the corps don't launch combat activity in Sarajevo itself but they focus on the implementation of the tasks in the framework of the Lukavica 93 operation which I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
