utterances.text: Thank you. In item 5 you say that better morale is felt overall after the successful taking of Trnovo and it is also mentioned that this is part of the Lukavac 93 operation?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's important to understand this correctly. When we entered Trnovo on the 18th of July, we must know that the Herzegovina Corps at the same time linked up with us in that area. So in this manner Herzegovina was connected with the remainder of Republika Srpska because from June 1992 after the beginning of their operation south 92, Herzegovina to the south of the Kalinovik-Foca axis was separated from the remainder of Republika Srpska. That is why this mention about the boost to morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see that the enemy fires six shells at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And two civilians got killed. I was not careful enough. You say up there that Vojkovic was fired at and below that you mention six shells fired on Grbavica, Lukavica and Dobrinja. We see down there that two civilians got killed. Where could this happen, the death of these two civilians?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no mention of the place where they got killed, but we know that Vojkovic and Grbavica were targeted so it must have been there. At the level of the Main Staff or even at the corps level, it is important to be informed of the overall civilian casualties, but it is also good to know where these events happened so that measures can be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3421, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D01569. This is still July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look at this and I will briefly summarise. It seems that from Pofalici and Kovaci they targeted Grbavica with mortars and recoilless gun as well as machine-guns and infantry weapons and one civilian was killed at Grbavica. Then from Hrasnica 82-millimetre shell were fired and under (b) you say that they broke the cease-fire. Was this a time of cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again we have the document on the screen for some period of time, Dr. Karadzic summarising the document before even beginning to put the question to the witness. I would suggest this is leading the witness and diminishes his responses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, we have been dealing with the incoming fire and responses, and although Mr. Karadzic used the word to summarise, but I take it to put the crux of the document and hearing from the witness. So what difficulty are you having with such exercise, if you could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The difficulty that I have, Your Honour, is that the witness with the document in front of him which he can read and with Dr. Karadzic's summarises has - and it's quite obvious because he's reading the document before he answers - ample time to formulate his answer based on what he reads in the document rather than from his recollection or his experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could I hear from you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think Dr. Karadzic is putting anything but the context to the witness so that he can comment on it appropriately. But I don't see anything wrong with putting a document before a witness and having the witness read the document, whether it refreshes their recollection, whether it evokes a comment. The point is not to ask a leading question once the document is before the witness but to put a document before a witness on the topic that he's already discussed to make it more precise, there's nothing wrong with him reading that document as it's -- in order to formulate his answer. That's not leading. Documents are put to witnesses all the time for them to see -- to refresh their recollection or give a comment on without it being considered a practice of leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's observation. I would allow the accused to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Dr. Karadzic, may we stress: Structure the questions in such a way that it isn't leading. This is the important thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try my best, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With regard to what was targeted, especially given the presence of UNPROFOR, how does this match your information about the exchange of fire and the events mentioned in this report?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must remind ourselves and remember that an order was given not to target the city. Here we see that the enemy is shooting from the city. We must also remember that at that time - this is the 25th of July - the Lukavac 93 operation is under way along the axes mentioned. So all enemy activity is focused on weakening the defence lines of the SRK at the Sarajevo front and slow down the attack on Trnovo, Bjelasnica, and Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell the Trial Chamber where Bistrik is and where Zetra is, the UNPROFOR headquarters. How can the fire from Bistrik hill directed at UNPROFOR be interpreted? Where is Zetra?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zetra is in Skenderija, I think. I'm not really familiar with all the details in Sarajevo. Bistrik is also in Sarajevo that is controlled by the BH Army Zetra was and Bistrik also under the control of the 1st Corps of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the conclusion and the -- and the outlook. It says that the enemy violates the cease-fire and tries to depict the activities as being the opposite of what they were by protesting with UNPROFOR and targeting UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Galic. Just a second. The interpreters didn't hear the last part of your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this match your experience with the behaviour of the opponent and what was the purpose of this shelling, that is, their shelling from their territory of UNPROFOR which was also in their territory? What do they want to achieve?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to lay the blame on the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3422, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There's another document from July, it's 1D01570.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at item number 1. Your deputy is providing information here about the intensity of fire targeting your territory by the enemy and that mortar fire was opened on UNPROFOR column from Hum and then under number 2 it says with regard to your units the order to cease-fire is strictly observed especially artillery fire and we fire back only in extreme necessity. Can you explain what the term "extreme necessity" means in this report?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the next page, but this was probably drafted by my Chief of Staff, Milosevic or someone who stood in for him. The purpose of this report was to say that they had received an order to observe the cessation of hostilities and attacks on the city, whereas on the other hand the enemy forces continued to attack from within the city. I don't see here that he wanted UNPROFOR to be informed about this but I think he should have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But what does it mean to respond only in extreme necessity? Can you say and explain to the Chamber what an extreme necessity is?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An extreme necessity is a very difficult decision for every commander or every human being for that matter, and that means that this is a situation when you have to defend your life. As far as a military unit is concerned, it means whether they're going to defend their positions or not. That constitutes an extreme necessity which forces them to respond and to thwart the enemy attack. When you have enemy artillery fire and if this is repetitive fire, then fire has to be returned in order to neutralise them and to prevent any further losses of own forces or to protect some crucial industrial facility. And we had many such facilities in the area of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3423, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D10576.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D10576.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now this is the month of August, General. The first few bullets speak about the targets, but I am interested in the period between 12.30 -- 20.30 and 22.00 hours where it says that the enemy was opening fire from Dobrinja 2 and 3 and constantly firing from Browning at the Lukavica Put [phoen] and Sucuri and also fired through grenades from a -- recoilless guns from Dobrinja 2 targeting the Sucuri neighbourhood. General, can you tell us what was the military purpose of firing these two grenades on private houses in Sucuri?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, speaking about what was happening on the front in general it is difficult to look at one incident in isolation. This was close to the end of Lukavac 93 operation and these houses in Sucuri and that area in general, as far as I remember there were no positions of ours. There were, though, some positions above the houses but of minor units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, it is stated in the indictment that if we fired one or two shells on the city that was with the purpose of terrorising the civilians. According to your knowledge, did the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps fire shells at areas, neighbourhoods, without any military purpose whatsoever solely with the intention of terrorising civilians?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of attacks aimed at terrorising civilians did not happen, they were never ordered, and I personally never received an order to carry out such attacks. Because terror begets terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see the consequences, Milenko Sucur was wounded and Slobodan Sucur was wounded when he tried to pull him out?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was another soldier. I don't know where you see that but I know that he was wounded while trying to pull out his comrades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is correct, General. Milenko Sucur was wounded, whereas Slobodan Sucur tried to pull him out and got wounded himself. Then it says there was no response to enemy provocation with the exception of repelling major attacks. Now, can you look at the sentence which speaks about UNPROFOR convoys which says that enemy opened fire from snipers but without any serious consequences.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please scroll up particularly the Serbian version because I don't see what you're talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last two lines.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was, so to speak, a frequent occurrence, to open fire on humanitarian columns and UNPROFOR columns and other convoys of a similar nature so this is nothing unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you look at conclusions and predictions, this is consistent with what you said, that the cease-fire was being violated and that UNPROFOR is being shot at with the aim of portraying that as being done by the Army of Republika Srpska and to influence the international public and cause the intervention of NATO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the question. We were still interpreting the previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters couldn't hear the last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often were they successful in these deceptions in creating an UNPROFOR -- an impression with UNPROFOR that it was the Serbian side opening fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From day one we discussed the provocations at length and I said that we used to call such operations - and I don't know whether the Muslims used the same term - but anyhow we used to call it step by step until intervention, which means by way of various provocations to provoke a response from the SRK and the Army of Republika Srpska and then portray the situation as their firing without any reason and need whatsoever. And one of these provocations was an attack on the UNPROFOR convoy, the UNHCR convoy, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D10584.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A while ago you spoke many times that you were entitled to respond by using the same type of weapons. Now, look at item 1, bullet 2, where it says that from the Srebrenik direction they attacked by PAT and PAM, an anti-aircraft machine-gun, and anti-aircraft gun; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you only use PAM instead of PAT as well?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that there was cease-fire which came into force sometime in August, I think on the 11th or the 14th when I withdrew from Igman. So that required very precise reporting on the breaches of the cease-fire and that is why you have very precise co-ordinates from the maps. The point why we used PAM, which is 12.7-millimetre anti-aircraft machine-gun and PAT is 12, the former is a more precise weapon in terms of returning fire, whereas an anti-aircraft machine-gun shell whenever it comes to the first obstacle it becomes fragmented. We all know how burst of fire is opened at an aircraft and if fire came from Sedrenik we only used a more precise weapon in order to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, from the point of view of collateral damage what is the difference between PAM fire and PAT fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, PAM fire should not, if it is precise, cause collateral damage. It should rather engage and destroy a military target. However, such losses are always possible. If the line of vision goes further on over residential area, it can overshoot, whereas in terms of the use of PAT the losses are greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now 1D01598.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in line 1 you can see that truce was in force but that the Muslims violated it, and then it says where this was done and so on and so forth. And then it says that 1615 hours a shell fell in Vrace and wounded a 13-year-old boy and a woman was wounded on Ozrenska Street. Now, what was the point of firing only one shell and what was the point of firing at this woman from a sniper rifle on Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an 82-millimetre shell which was fired on Vrace -- I have to tell you that in Vrace itself there were no positions or deployment of our troops. A little bit down there were some forces, though, but in Vrace itself there were no military targets at the time, whether they were aiming at something else I don't know, but as I say there were no military targets in Vrace at the time and that is why the casualty was civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then under item 2 you say that you did not respond to enemy provocations unless they threatened the positions and lives of your troops. Now, could this wounding of the young boy and this woman something that could be described as extreme necessity or is an extreme necessity only situation when the lives of your soldiers are at risk?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are heavy casualties, both military and civilian, but they cannot be categorised as an extreme necessity. If you have in mind loftier goals and if you take into consideration what are the repercussions of such a response, both internationally and with regard to the SRK, if you weigh these two options then it is better to refrain from opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Leave it at that. Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D01610.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we go back to this document. Item 2, so: "All units are formally holding positions, are generally not responding to enemy provocation except when the positions and the lives of our troops are in danger." Is it routine explanation what your units were doing or is it a specific explanation what your units did in relation to the fire which we see in the previous document -- passage? I'm not sure whether there was a return fire or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, as far as I can see, we can see from the report - and I cannot remember every single day and what was happening on every single day during two years in that zone. I also have to look at the report in order to be able to comment because I'm not a computer, I'm just human, and it's been 20 years. So we have to be reasonable when you are asking me to answer and when the questions are formulated. I would say that something is noted about our units here, namely, that they are on these positions, they're holding them, and not responding unless their lives are threatened. And we have seen from a report that there was one fatality so that there are lives which are threatened. Now, whether there was response in that specific area, I probably cannot now -- I suppose not because cease-fire was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, we are now already in October 1993 and under 1 it is stated here that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, now we have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the 13th of October under item number 1 as usual it is stated what the enemy is doing and at 1630 hours fired two 82-millimetre shells on Banjalucka Street from the direction of the railway station and also two shells on Moravska Street from the direction of the city. Can you tell us whether you had some military infrastructure targets or troops on Banjalucka and Moravska Streets?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that with any certainty right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sniper fire is also included in the report, and so on, and under item 2 in the report says that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps observed the cease-fire but periodically opened fire when the lives and positions of the soldiers were threatened. The units are surveying and so on and so forth. Compared with the previous report, is this one clearer or does this report say that there was some fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by this report we can conclude once again that we did not fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this, but periodically opened fire when the lives of the soldiers were threatened and the positions too?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But at which section and how much fire was returned, I cannot claim that they returned fire precisely in this location or in which location. I'm saying on the whole that we did not return fire except at specific points or sections of the front, as the report says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then it says that a group of officers and the Chief of Staff are in the field where they are conducting some controls. And then you say that one soldier was wounded by a sniper shot - that's the following page - one soldier was wounded. So what sort of a loss is that? How would you consider that, the loss of one wounded soldier?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would consider it an average loss. During a day when you have one wounded soldier that's an average loss. So it's not a major loss, we could not consider it as such, it is a loss but not a major one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what do you think was the purpose of firing two shells on Banjalucka and two on Moravska Street from the city?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you recently that I was not sure whether we had some troops deployed in that area at that specific moment, that point in time. As far as I know, they shouldn't have been there but I cannot claim that with certainty. I said that earlier so now I am repeating myself again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that is honest of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3427, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please have 1D01620. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 26th of October and under item 1, as in all reports, you inform about the areas that were targeted by shells, rifle grenades, sniper fire, PAM from Mojmilo, Dobrinja, and from the city. And then in Vogosca there was two mortar shells that were filled with chloride. How does that fit in with your knowledge and how often did they put -- how often did they put chlorine in the shells?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Chlorine" rather than "chloride."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember well the reports that -- which were sent at the time that there was chlorine and other chemicals that were used to fill those shells, namely. It was nothing new, as in our army, earlier on the Yugoslav People's Army, I mean, there were instances of preparations of various charges. So if chlorine was used, I know that they said there was some white trace and that later on fire was caused and so on. I think that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what sort of unrest happened in the city of Sarajevo which resulted in wounding of some people on our side? Can you remember what was happening in the city of Sarajevo in late October 1993 among themselves?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many things were going on then. That was the culmination of the events that had to do with their paramilitaries and para-commanders. That was the 26th of October, the day on which the commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade Musan Topalovic was killed. We know that in his -- his zone included Kazani as well and that that was where most Serbs perished, in that area. Later on he turned not only against the Serbs but also against his own people in his zone. He became too arrogant and he did not want to obey anyone anymore so they had to liquidate him, just as they took measures against other commanding officers. We know that immediately after that in 1993 the commander Sefer Halilovic was replaced, that in 1993 at the beginning of the year, or rather, in late 1992 Juka Prazina as someone from the Main Staff and a member of the paramilitaries, so to speak, went out to Igman and in 1993 when the conflict between the HVO and the BH Army broke out and later on he was killed somewhere around here in Belgium. This is squaring of accounts happened in the zone of the BH Army 1st Corps and this was one particular day on which that happened. It was one of the heavier conflicts in the zone of the BH Army 1st Corps. I could say much more but I think that what I have said is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did -- these two Muslims, the prisoners, wounded in Grbavica, in that chaos and unrest, did they continue to shoot in the direction of the Serb-held territories?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's probable that they not only -- they were in panic in Sarajevo, a general panic, the 1st Corps of the BH Army. And sometimes they acted in a confused manner: Who should they wage war against, against themselves or against us? And in such a situation they also fired on everything that was in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Under the conclusions you say in spite of internal unrest and turmoil in the city of Sarajevo the enemy forces are firing from various kinds of weapons on our positions on the confrontation line. Is this what you just told us that regardless of what was happening in the city they continued to fire at you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this confirms what I said previously in my previous sentence. I have nothing to add, nothing else, no comments. They are unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3428, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And again, for the record, it's a document not signed by the witness and, in fact, it doesn't appear to be signed by his behalf either in type script. It appears to be signed by Dragomir Milosevic. I don't know if that's General Milosevic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, who was authorised by you to sign the corps documents?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a special order and instructions on signing documents, who was entitled to sign which document. That's regulated, namely, who can sign for the commander. We can see here that my deputy was appointed, Colonel Dragomir Milosevic, but this is not his signature even though it does -- says M something, but as far as I remember this wasn't his signature. His signature was somewhat different. I don't know. Once again I emphasise that this is a report from the corps command and many times we will be in a situation in which the person who is supposed to sign the document, my deputy or the duty operations officer, and the duty officer at the command post is also authorised to sign a report sent to the superior command if the three persons I enumerated are absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please -- you already told us that you were fired at from the vicinity of certain facilities which should not be used for such activities. Were there any such incidents and where did they mostly occur, or rather, what were the sensitive facilities from the vicinity of which fire was opened at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most sensitive buildings and facilities which were abused - if I can call it that way - I can find no better and useful word than that were the premises of protected buildings and these were the premises of hospitals, schools, museums, the premises or areas where observation points of military observers of -- from the United Nations were deployed and where command posts of the UN HQ were also located, whether it was the sector command or the BH command. Because we know that the sector remained in Sarajevo practically throughout this time and the BH command later moved from Kiseljak to Sarajevo to the area that was within the zone of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. That's the location close to Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D01585.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not in chronological order really. This is from early September. Can you please note the first bullet under item 1, that an infantry attack was attempted from the direction of the Jezero hospital which was repelled. Did you know about this incident and do you know which unit of theirs was deployed at the Jezero hospital?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This hospital, Jezero, was not really operational so much at the time. Whether something was functioning there, whether any services were provided, I'm not sure. But the premises were protected anyway. They attacked it upwards in the direction of Mrkovici, I think, more or less. I think that was the axis, and I couldn't provide any more comments about that area, but I could say that it was a protected area, a protected facility in any case, but attacks were launched from that facilities towards our positions in the direction of Mrkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where the maternity ward was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it used to be a maternity ward, Jezero, but I'm not sure if anyone was giving birth there at the time. I didn't have sufficient information to be able to claim that that was still working at the time. I know that there was a maternity ward in that hospital, but I didn't point it out for what I said earlier, namely, that I didn't know whether the hospital was operational at the time and whether it provided such services or not, but I do know that there was a maternity ward precisely in that hospital, Jezero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A little further down it reads that forces are gathering at the faculty of transportation. Why was that faculty used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand, it was the students' village. We called it that. It was -- it remained behind after the Olympics 1994 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1984, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was used to deploy soldiers in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at item 8 where it says that provocations are continuing which leads to the exhaustion of soldiers but they responded in exceptional circumstances. How long they can restrain themselves. Please explain what this means how this restraint reflected on the morale of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the benefit of hindsight, or rather, in hindsight, it doesn't look so difficult. But under the conditions after time when the SRK waged war, this is easy to understand. We dealt with the Ilidza Brigade a lot and we saw that it was almost encircled. They can't go to the airport, they only had about 800 metres of length that they covered, and there was no influx of fresh forces. There was always the same people and they had to bear a lot of pressure. The 4th Corps of the BH Army - and we saw that was deployed - then we know what exhaustion means. Not only the soldiers were exhausted, I was exhausted and our officers too because it went on day and night. There is a no pause in combat activities. If I was able to sleep for two hours without anything happening which required my intervention, I was happy and everybody lived under very similar conditions. If shells fall around you each and every day and if you must -- if it's susceptible to being hit by sniper anywhere and the rations of food were modest and any kind of supply was modest, sometimes we also ran short of ammunition. I would like to remind you, although you know better than I do, that the BH Army had under its control the facilities to produce ammunition and weapons, Bugojno and other places. So we didn't have enough ammunition. That also contributed to mental fatigue. When you don't have reserves, be it reserves in manpower or mental reserves, then exhaustion grows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? I just have one more document to show before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3429, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06017, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we wait, General, please tell us in general what the losses during cease-fire -- the cease-fire were?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a great problem. During the cease-fires we sustained heavy losses. Now the question was how do we react and how do we get both the soldiers and the civilians to obey, to be patient, and without excessive response, especially in case of civilian losses. And this -- those civilians are the relatives of the soldiers at the front line. There were no other soldiers but locals there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was a red document on the screen, 1D06017. This is not the one. A minute ago it was the right document, 1D06017. This is it. General, please tell us what is this list of shells fired by the enemy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- during these two months of cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's what I'm wondering, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should be one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I supposed to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court says there's none.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you try again? I believe that it can be uploaded. But if you prefer to have the break now, then we can wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, can you upload the previous document, last page. Exhibit D3429. Second page, number 8, conclusion. In English there are two 6's so number 7 should be number 8. Here at the end of the conclusion, General, I think it is a document signed for you by somebody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is -- this may have been signed by Lugonja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last sentence in the first paragraph of point number 8 it says: "... the question coming increasing to the forefront is how long they can restrain themselves." What does it mean? What would they do if they can't restrain themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can answer. Here's what this is about, Mr. President. We are informing the Main Staff in what military situation the units are and in what situation with regard to morale. If we continue to restrain ourselves, then there could be unauthorised, random fire from soldiers trying to protect their homes and families and children. That was to be expected if this fire is continued and if the 1st Corps of the BH Army begins moving its units. Through the UN, through the Supreme Command, we wanted to communicate that the enemy has to stop his actions and that the cease-fire proclaimed must be honoured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So was this a kind of notice to the Main Staff that there might be in the future some unrestrained firing from your units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a warning to the Main Staff and we also had information that soldiers and civilians are becoming increasingly impatient in order to prevent unwanted consequences. They had to take military and political measures to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you give us the example of military and political measures to prevent that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, political measures certainly include the crafting of an agreement to see what will happen in Sarajevo for us to have some prospect not just continue dying for nothing. And the world and everybody should learn about the situation in the areas held by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Our struggle should not be vilified. We should be allowed to defend ourselves. As for the military aspect, a new agreement can be reached and the commanders can reach agreement. I was never present at a meeting with representatives of the BH Army, I was never a member of commissions or delegations that met to take care of such issues. I therefore have no experience with that, but I know what they should do. If such incidents happen, I know that under article -- some article of annex 1, what must be done and what reports must be submitted for such actions to be punished, if no measures are taken, what can we expect? I hope this was enough; if not, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you yourself take any measures to prevent such event unrestrained response, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, I did take measures. You see here in my reporters that the command inspects units and they speak about the importance of the cessation of such actions. I tried to explain the importance of these cease-fire agreements and the cessation of all negative things happening in a war. It's not only a problem whether someone shot at the enemy or at this or that. The problem is within the unit to create moral and political conditions for such tasks to be carried out and the obligations connected with that to be honoured. I showed which measures we took, what we did to prevent unwanted consequences, from orders I issued with regard to the honouring of the Geneva Conventions, to the prohibition of targeting civilians, and also here when an order was issued to cease-fire at the town this must be respected. I think that even today we saw such orders. We also took a number of other measures to create better conditions on both sides. Mr. President, I believe that this will be discussed later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only, if I may, on page 69, line 7, of the transcript it was omitted in the witness's reply: "We did not reply to fire. We refrained from responding to fire." [In English] It says: "If we continue to restrain ourselves," that should be "from responding," or, "responding on fire then there could be unauthorised ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Galic, do you confirm that? You repeated -- after having said restrain ourselves and refrain from -- I'm sorry -- and refrain from responding on fire. I think it's -- it does not change much and it's the same meaning. I don't see any problem. We'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be checked against the tapes and then we'll know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 3.30 -- I'm sorry, 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.43 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the Presiding Judge asked you which measures you had undertaken in order to prevent the exhaustion and the tempting of patience which would be contrary to the order to restrain. Do you think that your response to the Main Staff constitutes one of the measures, one of the preventive measures?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understood your question, Mr. President. Well, the point is and I already said that a whole host of measures and activities taken by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in order to resolve the conditions of war and the conditions in which tasks had to be performed in conformity with the orders, definitely one of the ways to do that was to inform the Main Staff so that they could assist us in solving these problems. I think it would be worthwhile to mention here that you yourself were very much interested in many problems faced by the SRK and how they were being dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from informing the Main Staff and issuing orders to subordinate commands, did you take any other steps or did you communicate with the soldiers in any way in order to incite them to refrain from acting and to abide by the orders?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the activities that the corps was involved in during my testimony. One of such activities was touring the units along the front line and having meetings with the local authorities in the area of responsibility of the SRK in order to find solutions to the problems that were affecting both the civilians and soldiers in the area of their municipality. Then measures were also taken with a view to maintaining the situation that would enable the orders to be carried out to inform all the units up to the last soldier. Of course I couldn't accomplish that physically, but I did manage to tour some segments of the front line and certain axes. I think that that was quite sufficient. I also briefed commands to work with the soldiers and with their subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within the framework of this latter activity did you issue any declarations to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I communicated with all the soldiers by issuing declarations and I did that as well with civilians in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. This declaration that I sent both to the soldiers of my corps and other soldiers was intended to motivate them in order to be able to endure all the problems and difficulties they were facing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D06331, and I apologise that there is no translation yet but we are going to highlight the main points. So 1D06331.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what this is and we can see that this was drafted by you.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the way of communicating the entire force in the area of the SRK and it was primarily addressed to officers, non-commissioned officers, and ordinary soldiers. I presume that this type of proclamation reached the government authorities as well and that it prompted them to help us carry out our tasks. What was the need for such a proclamation? It was definitely required because we anticipated at the time with regard to the cease-fire that went into force on the 10th of June, 1994, that I felt the need to address all members of the corps so that all these relevant tasks can be completed to the full. I cannot comment now this proclamation from various aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the second paragraph speaks about the need to abide by the cease-fire of the 10th of June, 1994?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This related to refraining for one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then further below it says: "Demonstrate restraint at all provocations coming from the Muslims and respond only if you -- entirely necessarily and if approved by the Main Staff." Does this coincide with the way you acted?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is yet another proof that this was in compliance with the orders from the Main Staff because I invited all the forces to display restraint until situation of extreme necessity arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, put a pause and please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph -- the first sentence in the last paragraph, what are you asking them to do?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used a kind of colloquial refrain: Let us give up on alcohol, maybe it's difficult to translate into English, and refrain from alterations and inter party competition and rivalry. What I wanted to say was that one of the problems that might arise was alcohol, then there were internal rifts and conflicts that were not so numerous but they did occur, nevertheless, in various forms starting from political affiliations all the way to the way in which tasks should be performed. Here I said that this inter party political rifts should be left for some other period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the very bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here Captain Aleksic. What does it mean? It's handwritten. Does it mean that -- can we please lower the page?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see this note written by Captain Aleksic, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read the first sentence so that we know who you are addressing?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officers, non-commissioned officers, and soldiers, which means the entire force of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you explain this Captain Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document was drafted by him [as interpreted] probably he either drafted it or he had it, but it could have been in the hands of any member of the SRK or, for that matter, any member of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is a mistake in transcript. Aleksic was not the one who drafted it because the General said that he received it.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drafted it myself. I know exactly how I drafted it. You can criticise me if I didn't do a good job, but my intentions were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify. You said that every soldier should have one copy of this and that this probably came from Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each copy of this proclamation should be held by every soldier. I don't know the provenance of this proclamation and who wanted to show it, but I say, just as Captain Aleksic had it, it was accessible to every soldier including the soldiers from the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3440, Your Honours -- I'm sorry, 3430.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe I didn't hear properly. I had the feeling that General Galic was talking about all the soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think General had said so and it's reflected as such in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to repeat, Mr. President, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in that spirit - now it's difficult for me to repeat it word for word - but what I said more or less was that this proclamation was addressed to each soldier, commander, non-commissioned and commissioned officers of the SRK, but I do not rule out the possibility that it could have reached any member of the BH Army in the area of the SRK. That was my meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am not sure this is 3440. Anyway, can we have 1D06017, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have now the English translation? Hopefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, somebody compiled this on your behalf. This is a review of what you had to sustain during the two-month period of cease-fire and it says here in the area of Grbavica 101 shells. How big is the area of Grbavica and what was the impact and effects of 101 shells in the area such as Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you understand that this was only during the two months of cease-fire, it turns out that some 20 shells were fired on a monthly basis or one every day or two in October. If you take that Grbavica is an area stretch in between Debelo Brdo and Hrasno Brdo all the way down to the Miljacka river, then we can see that this area is not a big one. It is, perhaps, 5 by 5 kilometres approximately, maybe a bit larger. I never measured it. But earlier I said that this was a very compact area and it was exposed to the fire from city because one can descend from Vrace towards Miljacka and this road, particularly the main road leading to the Miljacka river, was constantly targeted not only by artillery and mortars but mostly by snipers and other weapons. So it was a very dangerous road. Such intensity of fire is tiring for the manpower and it causes losses. And it also speaks that the 1st Corps of the BH Army failed to observe the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please, in both English and Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here just to shorten it we can see that there was sniper fire, but the total is 1.420 [as interpreted] shells and a lot of infantry ammunition. And to see what were the casualties, 24 soldiers have been killed, 37 have been seriously wounded and 25 slightly wounded, so it's 49, 76, and 25, 190, 91 -- no, 101; right? 101. So you lost 101 soldiers. They were no longer able to fight. They were wounded or killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was what the calculation showed at the time, but we lost actually 24 soldiers. We had 37 seriously wounded. The slightly wounded were probably provided with assistance and then returned into combat. There was not much time for anyone to recuperate nor was there anyone who could stand in for them. So it should be counted that these were the losses from the operations. If we take into account that a series of measures were taken at the time in order to protect the troops, that they shouldn't fire, that they should keep as much time in dugouts and shelters, then these were still quite big losses for two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The two months of truce?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two months of truce rather than two months of combat, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3431, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember an incident with three mortar shells which fell in Alipasino Polje on the 22nd of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: January and February 1994, I could not say I don't remember them, but was that precisely the time when the areas you mentioned were targeted or not? I'm not sure on the basis of what you are asking me this question. What was the exact date? I would like to know that because just to say it like this is a bit too general. I cannot -- I can answer but my answer will be imprecise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will then try to be more specific. In the indictment I am charged with the fact that our forces in the area of Alipasino Polje fired three mortar shells on the 22nd of January, 1994. The first one in the park behind the residential building in Geteova Street number 3 that was earlier Cetinska Street, then earlier Klare Cetkin, and a third which fell in front of the buildings where the children were playing. Four children were killed, five adults were wounded, and according to the indictment, fire was opened from the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, that is to say the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, approximately from the direction of the west.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the names of the streets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness [sic] were not able to hear your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was probably the interpreter who was unable to hear me. Let me just see what I did say. I did present what this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On that 22nd of January, did you order that three mortar shells be fired on Alipasino Polje and did you receive a report that someone from your units from the west, the west to Alipasino Polje, fired these three shells if it was not you who did it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time and in that area, as far as I remember, no order was issued to fire on Alipasino settlement or Alipasino Polje. There were later various conjectures whether somebody else fired rather than the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. That was what I heard later during the war, not now. This section of Alipasino Polje -- we have to take into account that it was part of the zone of the BH army's 1st Corps and that their units were stationed in that area from one which was called Kulin Ban, as far as I remember, and whether that was the reason why fire was opened I'm not -- I don't think so from this point in time because a cease-fire was in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now have D2806, a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a regular combat report dated the 23rd. Let us please focus on the conduct of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The beginning of item 2 says that units are in full combat-readiness, they have stepped up surveillance and reconnaissance of the enemy, and under item 8 it says a decision for further operations remains unchanged. It is to be expected that the enemy will continue with provocations against our units with the -- aimed at causing incidents for which they intend to blame the Serbian side. Can you tell us what was the decision which remains unchanged?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the 23rd of January, 1994. The decision at the time was that the corps units be engaged to protect the Serbian territory and defend the Serbian area and Serbian territory together with the population in the area covered by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Nothing special was happening at that particular period, as far as I remember. A bit earlier we had to fortify our positions up in the area of Zuc, and so on, but that was before this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive a report about this incident or a protest lodged by the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have D964. D964, please. It is a Defence exhibit which has been admitted. Or I can read it out, but the participants should know what I'm reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do have the Serbian version now. The English version, just to make sure that it is matching, and then we'll move to the next page, as in the Serbian version it is on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document from the 1st Corps of the BH Army. They are reporting the staff about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Can we briefly go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is a report of the 1st Corps to their Supreme Command Staff about discussion with this UN general. Please have a look at the last paragraph. If we could also show the second page in English it says that the deputy commander objected to UNPROFOR's statement related to a massacre on Alipasino Polje in regards to which this general replied that they couldn't determine the exact position the shells came from on the basis of their traces. According to the information you had, General, if they could not establish where the shells had come from, was that the reason why they did not address this matter with you?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be one of the reasons, certainly, because if they did not establish something there was always a problem with those protests. I always told them: If you lodge a protest, please give me a sketch from the on-site investigation so that I can react properly rather than you just come to see me and say this and that happened. What can I do on the basis of that? It's a major problem. How can I respond to such requests? I suppose that he did not have sufficient elements to address me about the problem and that was why I was not informed about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last question of yours was very leading, I have to note, albeit belated. Shall we admit it? We'll admit it as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3432, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And my colleague sitting beside me established that he's fallible and identified where this was previously used in court and indeed your proposal was very well-placed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just add something else here with regard to this document and this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, nothing to do with that, something quite different, what we did and what is mentioned here. I think that General Milosevic probably testified about that too. At the time we were working on the anti-sniping agreement and let me just say before this Tribunal and this Chamber that that idea was an idea of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to conclude that agreement. It was concluded on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the General please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was concluded by General Milosevic just as I was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to that topic. Can you please tell us, General, how we were portrayed in the Muslim media with regard to various incidents? And I specifically have in mind the incident which occurred on the 4th of February in the Dobrinja settlement, where, according to the indictment, three mortar shells, 120-millimetre shells, were fired which in Oslobodilaca Sarajeva Street in a line for humanitarian aid caused some casualties. How did we generally and particularly -- portrayed in connection with these incidents in the Sarajevo media?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time rather many such incidents occurred and they were the basis for accusing the SRK and the VRS in general. Starting from the incident in January followed by this one on the 4th of February and there was another on the 5th. Why was that done? The one who did it, who caused these incidents, can only be an enemy of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Serbian people. That is why all the propaganda of the time directed against the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Army of Republika Srpska and the problems that were happening and from which side the shell or the -- or another explosive device was fired, lodged, the very fact that something of this kind can happen in that situation. When we withdrew from Igman and Bjelasnica, when we said nothing significant would happen, why cause such losses? I see no reasons and no justification no matter who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you on the 4th of February order fire at the queue of people waiting for humanitarian aid at Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And if I may add, I had been informed of this incident and I had taken measures already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of measures? What did you find out?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we said about Alipasino Polje, that I wasn't informed, here on the contrary I received some information. I was not at the corps command at the time, but we got information that the incident had happened and then we demanded subordinate units to report on what had happened and state whether they had opened fire at the time and targeted that area. I believe that was the essence of what they wanted then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get D1515.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is already an exhibit. It's a report to the Main Staff dated the 4th of February. Somebody signed on your behalf because I don't think this is your signature. Let us take a look at the bottom of the page. A convoy of Jews and then it further, or rather, in one bullet point up concerning the alleged targeting of Dobrinja with 82-millimetre shells, what was -- which was published by Muslim TV and the radio. The group for co-operation did not receive any protests from UNPROFOR and it was found out that no fire was opened at the Dobrinja sector. Officially now was issued by the Republika Srpska news media with the approval and according to the instructions of the Main Staff of the VRS. Do you stand by this today?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I was not at the command post at the time, but I assume full responsibility for this. I thought that they had received a protest, but this clearly states that they had only gotten the information through the media. When you get information from the media, there's a risk involved in any checks. But still, they did check with the units and the units said that they hadn't opened fire. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience, what would your conclusion be? Why did the UNPROFOR not launch an official protest?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that UNPROFOR at the time did not submit a protest in connection with this incident because it didn't have enough information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to Markale, that is, the 5th of February, 1994. In my indictment and probably yours it is alleged that one 120-millimetre mortar shell hit the open-air market known as Markale in the old city of Sarajevo, a civilian area. The indictment reads that the market-place was full of people and 66 people were killed, whereas more than 140 were wounded. It is alleged that fire was opened from positions in the north-east. Let's go step by step. And be brief in your answers, please. Did you on the 5th of February issue an order for a shell to be fired at the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never have ordered to target the market because we preserved that market for four or five years. After all that, issuing an order to fire at it would have been absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you get information from subordinate units that a lower-ranked commander ordered this fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you check the matter and what did you find out?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was -- this is what the situation was like. General Gvero was at the airport talking to the Muslim side and UNPROFOR, and he demanded that a commission be established to investigate the incident. This was said at my trial too. But the Muslim side and UNPROFOR refused, as usual, because they said they could not guarantee the safety of the commission if the members of the SRK, that is, Serbs, were part of that commission. So that nobody from our side took part in the work of that commission. Ten commissions investigated the Markale incident, which is what I learned only later, but they were unable to officially establish where the shell had come from. With that I want to say if ten commissions are unable to determine exactly what happened, how should we, if we were not even present - and this applies to some other incidents as well -- I think you asked me what we did later, what else we did. From the reports that I read after returning to the corps command, I learned that a commission or some body was established to inspect the units and even go there and I remember a remark that they find out in the area of Mrkovici where there was some waters and it was snowing at the time. The hood or the tarp which is placed on the mouth of the mortar was covered with snow. So it was impossible for a shell to be fired from there. This is what we were able to find out, although we were not allowed to take part in the work of those commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you accept the allegation that over 200 people were hit by one shell and that there were even more people at the market-place on a winter afternoon? What was your conclusion from these facts?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say how many people there were, 200 or 50 or whatever, but it was winter-time and there should probably have been fewer people there. That's my assumption. And for one 120-millimetre mine to inflict such casualties, well that would make it a unique shell in the whole world. According to our estimates of the losses caused by one single 120-millimetre shell, these losses are certainly deplorable, that's all what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you think it was possible that there was so many people and that so many got killed by one shell, so many people among stalls and other obstacles?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was put forward at the trial and elsewhere later, but it's difficult to accept as accurate and that really everything happened as described. I'm especially interested in a detail because I would like this incident to be investigated so as to show who's responsible. Where are the fragments of the shell? We saw the tail of the shell, but these can be found anywhere. But there are no fragments to be found anywhere. They were only shown in pictures, but the fragments themselves are nowhere to be found. And there are other elements of a technical nature and of a general nature, including the overall situation that make this quite abnormal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was any agreement struck after the incident with regard to the positioning of large-calibre weapons in the Sarajevo zone?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the only agreement where I was involved in the talks together with you. I remember it still. On the 18th we worked with Akashi, Rose, and all the others, and somehow we got some information. I arrived around the 11th. And the information was that this part of the incident was caused by the BH Army and in a way General Rose also admitted as much when he made his statement. However, he said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence about the two persons he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Galic, the interpreters couldn't hear your last sentence, "However ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't finish. What did Rose say?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I repeat now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Rose said that he first stated that the BH Army was to blame for the incident, but later he explained that in the following fashion that he only said as much to pressure Alija into talks because Alija constantly refused talks, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Bench what the essence of the agreement reached on the 18th of February was and whether the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps honoured the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes -- just a second. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's just a small thing, but the witness -- the witness hasn't said anything about the date that Dr. Karadzic put some words in his mouth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I did say the 18th that the president and I were together with General Rose and the others at that meeting, and that was the first time I was present when an agreement was reached. I said that earlier. You can check the transcript. I'm positive that I said it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 95, line 15, or rather, page 90, line 15 "the 18th" was omitted but the witness certainly did say it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that I said it but I didn't check whether it was noted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was the essence and did the corps, commanded by you, implement the agreement?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The essence of the agreement was for all heavy weapons from calibre 12.7 millimetres up be pulled out to at least 20 kilometres from the centre of Sarajevo, which applied to both sides, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the BH Army. The assets which could not be pulled out because they were damaged or because the dead-line was too short, I believe the dead-line was by midnight on the 19th. I don't have it before me to be sure, but the order was that everything that hadn't been pulled out or reported would be targeted by NATO planes. The purpose of the agreement was to reduce losses on both sides and probably to create better conditions for a peaceful resolution in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps honour the agreement and did the BH Army 1st Corps honour it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
